name: Cadmium Orange
lede: Cadmium Orange is a pigment made from cadmium sulphide, a rich, opaque and sun-proof orange of the nineteenth century, and the name that now also stands for a warm orange hue.

sections.title: Two meanings of the name
sections.body:
Cadmium Orange names a pigment first and a hue second [8]. As a pigment it is cadmium sulphide, sometimes with selenium in it, ground into oil or watercolor [8][6]. As a hue it is a warm, medium-light orange, the swatch here being #ED872D [13].

The two meanings have drifted apart. Ball notes that paints labelled Cadmium Red or Cadmium Orange are now often colored with organic molecules, so that the name has gone from describing a composition to describing a hue [5]. The page you are reading is about both: the metal and its sulphide, and the color people still ask for by the old name.

sections.title: From a zinc works to a color
sections.body:
The element came out of a factory. In 1817 the German chemist Friedrich Stromeyer noticed a yellow oxide as a by-product at a zinc works in Salzgitter, and analysis showed a new metal [1]. The word *cadmia* was an old name for zinc ore, and the new element was named from it [1]. Greenockite, the cadmium sulphide mineral, is named for Lord Greenock [8].

Stromeyer made the bright yellow sulphide himself, and by 1819 he was writing that its beauty and fixity promised well for painting [1]. He also found that changing the conditions of the reaction could produce an orange material instead, and that grain size controls which hue results [1]. The Pigment Compendium adds that the sulphide's hue runs from lemon yellow to orange-red depending on the structure of the colloidal aggregates [6].

sections.title: A pure orange at last
sections.body:
Until the nineteenth century a painter had no strong, pure orange to buy. Realgar leaned toward yellow, and chrome orange, from the alkaline route to lead chromate described by Vauquelin, was the first pure and powerful orange artists had met [3]. Ball says that before this time there was no good pure orange pigment, and no good violet either [2].

The nineteenth-century color chemist George Field made cadmium orange his example of a pure pigment [2]. In his book *Chromatography* he argued that an original pigment is purer and more durable than a mixture of red and yellow, and gave cadmium orange as his case [2]. A real orange pigment absorbs almost none of the orange part of the spectrum, which is why a mixed orange looks duller beside it [2].

sections.title: Scarce metal, slow start
sections.body:
The supply was the problem. Zinc smelting did not produce enough cadmium for the yellow to make an impact before the 1840s [1]. Ball finds evidence of cadmium yellow in French and German oil painting from about 1829, no sign of it in the lists of English paint makers in 1835, and production by Winsor and Newton by 1851 [1]. Paterson gives 1820 as the year cadmium yellow was first made, earlier than the evidence of use in oil painting from about 1829 that Ball cites; the books do not reconcile the two dates [8][1].

As to orange, Salter wrote in 1869 that cadmium orange was introduced to the art world at the International Exhibition in London in 1862, and says little more about it [6]. That agrees with Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930, which dates the color name to 1862 [13]. Field remarked in 1870 that cadmium yellow was little used because the metal was scarce, its cost passing to the pigment [1].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
Claude Monet used cadmium yellow extensively from at least 1873, and Ball suggests his example may have encouraged Manet and Morisot [1]. The Pigment Compendium reports the amorphous form of cadmium sulphide on many paintings by Monet, and notes that it has darkened in some where it was mixed with chrome yellow [7].

Orange entered the modern palette. Monet's *Impression, Sunrise* of 1872 has a small orange sun in a blue mist; Coles names its pigment as chrome orange, and says the later, more stable cadmium orange fixed the color in the modern palette [10][9]. Set against blue, its complement, the chrome and cadmium pigments produced the contrasts used by Toulouse-Lautrec, Munch, Gauguin and Van Gogh [9][2].

sections.title: The sulphide-selenide family
sections.body:
Cadmium orange is one member of a family. Replacing some of the sulphur with selenium moves the color from yellow through orange to red, and mercury or zinc in place of cadmium gives orange to maroon [7]. The Pigment Compendium gives a selenium to cadmium ratio of 10 to 90 for orange shades, 20 to 80 for bright red and 30 to 70 for dark maroon [7].

The Colour Index lists cadmium orange under three constitution numbers: 77196 for the selenide, 77199 for the sulphide and 77201 for cadmium mercury sulphide [6]. The first two are also Pigment Orange 20, the third Pigment Orange 23, and some commercial cadmium oranges are an impure selenide [6]. Gurney's table of modern oranges lists cadmium orange beside benzimidazolone, perinone, pyrrole and quinacridone oranges [12].

sections.title: The red it led to
sections.body:
Cadmium red is basically cadmium yellow with selenium in place of the sulphur, and selenium was found in 1817, the same year as cadmium [4]. Because deep cadmium orange blurs into red, the origin of the red is hard to trace. Field praised a cadmium red in 1869 that he called orange-scarlet, which Ball takes to be only a particularly deep cadmium orange [4].

No document specifying the sulphide-selenide is known before a German patent of 1892, and the red was not a commercial product until 1910; Bayer improved its manufacture in 1919 [4]. Paterson also dates cadmium red to 1910 [8]. Matisse tried in 1904, without success, to persuade Renoir to take up cadmium red in place of vermilion; Ball thinks he meant Field's orangey kind, closer to [[vermilion]] than the deep modern pigment [4].

sections.title: Toxicity and the end of the name
sections.body:
Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal, though Ball says only mildly so, and the colors pose no great hazard to the painter [5]. Concern about heavy metals in the environment is bringing tighter restrictions, and a complete ban in paints has been debated [5]. Paterson notes that its use is in decline because of cadmium's scarcity and toxicity [8].

If a ban comes, quinacridones, sold since 1958, are the most promising substitutes [5]. That is how a pigment name becomes a hue name: the label stays, the chemistry changes.

sections.title: Swatches and neighbors
sections.body:
Our swatch comes from the library entry for Cadmium Orange, #ED872D, which cites Wikipedia and ISCC-NBS 1955 block 48 [13]. Ridgway recorded the name in 1886 and again in his 1912 atlas (plate III, hue 13), where the aged-plate scan reads #FE7F17, about 13 CIELAB units away (our calculation) [13]. Both are screen approximations of a paint, not the paint itself.

The app's nearest named color is [[tangerine]], 3 units away, and the family names are [[orange]], [[pumpkin]], [[mandarin-orange]], [[persian-orange]] and [[burnt-orange]] [13]. Its cadmium cousins are [[cadmium-lemon]], [[cadmium-green]] and [[light-cadmium]] [13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color match to this swatch appears in 60 paintings, 0.25 per cent, which makes it more common than 54 per cent of named colors (as photographed) [14]. Inside a painting it is an accent in 92 per cent of the 71 paintings where we find it, by lightness rank within each painting [14].

India stands out. Six of 721 Indian paintings carry it, and the Pahari school has it at 19.5 times the expected rate and the Rajput school at 15.8 times, among them [[painting:cma-314236|Krishna celebrates Holi]] [14]. The color's closest company in the archive is ochre, 21 paintings at 13 times the expected rate [14]. Across the archive the 1820s peak at 7.4 times the expected rate, decades before the pigment's recorded introduction, so those matches are other oranges, not cadmium [14]. A later picture with a large patch is Bonnard's [[painting:commons-Q17491092|Corner of a table]] of 1935 [14].

The earliest dated painting with at least 2 per cent of the canvas in this color is Masaccio's *The Madonna of Humility* of 1423, which is 463 years before the name's earliest record in our sources [14]. That is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a cadmium pigment, and the archive's early centuries are thin [14]. Photographs of aged, varnished paintings cannot tell a pigment from a lookalike.

questions.q: Why was the orange of cadmium orange more vibrant than a mixture of red and yellow paints?
choices: It is a true orange pigment that does not absorb the orange part of the spectrum
It was always thinned with white
It was ground finer than other paints
It was a dye, not a pigment
questions.answer: It is a true orange pigment that does not absorb the orange part of the spectrum

questions.q: What does adding selenium in place of some sulphur do to cadmium sulphide?
choices: Moves it from yellow toward orange and red
questions.answer: Moves it from yellow toward orange and red

questions.q: True or false: the earliest painting in our archive matching this orange (1423) proves cadmium pigment existed then.

openers: Cadmium orange came out of a zinc works: Stromeyer found the metal there in 1817, and changing the grain size of its sulphide turned yellow into orange.
Paint labelled cadmium orange today is often organic: the name has moved from the chemistry to the hue.
Look for it as an accent: in 92 per cent of the paintings where our archive finds it, it plays the smallest, brightest part.
